750.title: Kabir's mother weeps
750.hook: in one hymn his mother cries that her son sings of the Lord instead of weaving (Gujri, Kabir)
750.tomorrow: The elephant that would not charge
750.howItsDone: Sikhs sing this Gujri hymn of Kabir in kirtan, and teachers often pair it with the Gurus' call to honest work, so the hymn is heard as devotion, not as a reason to stop earning.

segments.voice: Yesterday, warp and weft, and your line, woven. Did you follow one thread until it slipped under another? Today the loom goes quiet, and someone notices. Day seven hundred fifty.

The loom has stopped. In a small house in Kashi there's no clack of the shuttle today, and no cloth to take to market. There are children to feed. And in the next room, a woman is crying quietly, the kind of crying that tries not to be heard. Her son, the weaver, is singing again. Not working. Singing about the Lord. The remarkable thing is who tells us this scene. It's Kabir himself, in a hymn that sits in the Guru Granth Sahib. He sets his own mother's tears inside his song. Today: Kabir's mother weeps.
screen: `THE LOOM HAS STOPPED.` → `CHILDREN TO FEED.` → `HIS MOTHER, CRYING.`

segments.voice: The hymn is in Raag Gujri. It opens with her: Kabir's mother sobs and sobs, and asks the Lord how these children will live. Kabir, she says, has given up weaving and spinning, and written the Lord's name on his body. Stop there a moment. She isn't a villain in this story. She's doing the sums. A weaver who doesn't weave has no cloth, and no cloth means no food. It is the arithmetic of anyone lying awake over rent. Kabir doesn't mock her for it. He puts her tears first, before his own answer, so her side is heard first. Then he speaks. As long as he's passing thread through the bobbin, he says, he forgets the Lord he loves. The work keeps pulling his mind away. And the hymn ends with Kabir turning to her, gently: listen, my mother, the one Lord is the giver, for me and for these children too. That's the whole answer. Not, stop worrying. Not, you don't understand. Just: the same Giver holds all of us. Sikh readers hold this hymn with care. The Gurus taught honest work as part of the path, so it isn't read as permission to quit your job. It's read as a picture of a heart so full of the Name that the loom couldn't hold it, and of a son who still answers his mother tenderly. Today's line comes out of that answer. Mother, he's weaving love. The cloth has changed, and the thread is still running.
screen: `RAAG GUJRI: HER TEARS COME FIRST.` · `SHE'S DOING THE SUMS.` · `THE BOBBIN PULLS HIS MIND AWAY.` · `ONE GIVER, FOR ALL OF US.` · then, large: `MOTHER, HE'S WEAVING LOVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: forgive a worried parent. Or a grandparent, or whoever worried over you. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one time their worry came out sideways: a sharp word, a nagging question, a fear about your choices. Now look underneath it, the way Kabir did. What were they counting? Food, safety, your future? Let the worry be what it was, sums done late at night. If forgiving feels too big today, just soften toward them by one notch. If you pray, you can hold their name with Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
Kabir's mother weeps. A hymn in Raag Gujri where Kabir sets his mother's tears first, and answers her: one Lord is the giver for us all.
Your line: mother, he's weaving love. Today, when someone worries at you, hear the sums underneath before you answer, and answer gently. Day seven hundred fifty.

751.title: The elephant that would not charge
751.word: The elephant that would not char
751.hook: Kabir sings of being bound and thrown before an elephant that bowed instead (Gond, Kabir, ang 870)
751.howItsDone: Sikhs sing Kabir's Gond hymn of the elephant in kirtan, and katha tellers retell it as a story of a devotee's steadiness before power.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kabir's mother weeps, and your line, mother, he's weaving love. Did you hear the sums under someone's worry? Today the weaver faces something far bigger than a worried mother. Day seven hundred fifty-one.

His arms are tied. He's been bundled up like a sack and thrown down on the ground. Across the yard, a man sits high on an elephant's neck with a goad in his hand, and an official is shouting at him to drive it forward. The elephant is huge. The man on the ground is a weaver. Everyone watching knows how this is supposed to end. Except it doesn't. The one who tells us so is the man in the bundle. Kabir sings it himself, in a hymn in Raag Gond. Today: the elephant that would not charge.
screen: `ARMS TIED, THROWN DOWN.` → `THE DRIVER RAISES THE GOAD.` → `IT DOESN'T END THAT WAY.`

segments.voice: Here's how the hymn tells it. They bound his arms and threw him down like a lump. The driver, in anger, struck the elephant on the head. But the elephant turned and ran, crying out, as Kabir hears it, I am a sacrifice to this form of the Lord. The official, whom the hymn calls the qazi, the judge, shouts at the driver: drive it on, or I'll cut you down. The elephant won't move. The hymn says it stands still in meditation, because the Lord lives in its heart. Then Kabir asks the question at the center: what wrong has this saint done, that you tied him in a bundle and gave him to the elephant? And the line that gives us today's carry: the elephant lifts the bundle again and again, and bows to it. The judge, Kabir says, was in the dark and didn't see. Sikhs hold this hymn in more than one way. Some take it just as it's sung, a wonder that really happened to Kabir. Others hear the elephant as a picture too: the huge, angry force of the world, which, faced with someone whose heart rests in the Lord, can't find its target. Both readings end in the same place, the hymn's own last line. Kabir says the Lord of the world is mine, and the devotee's life rests in the fourth state. Notice what Kabir doesn't do in the song. He doesn't fight, and he doesn't curse the judge. He stays, and the elephant bowed.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stay calm before a big thing. Choose one thing ahead of you that feels like an elephant: a hard conversation, a test, a bill, a diagnosis, a deadline. Settle, and breathe. Let it stand there in your mind, full size. Don't shrink it, and don't run. Just breathe slowly in its presence, and feel your feet on the ground. Let your breath stay as steady as the man in the bundle. If you pray, you can rest one Waheguru on each slow breath. The bell holds the time.
The elephant that would not charge. Kabir's hymn in Raag Gond: bound and thrown before an elephant, which turned away and bowed to him instead.
screen: `THE ELEPHANT THAT WOULD NOT CHARGE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the elephant bowed. Today, when something big comes at you, stand still for one breath before you react, and watch what it does. Day seven hundred fifty-one.

752.title: If you're a Brahmin
752.hook: Kabir asks, if birth made you high, why weren't you born by some other road (Gauri, Kabir, ang 324)
752.howItsDone: Sikhs sing this Gauri hymn of Kabir in kirtan, and teachers connect it with langar and the Gurus' rejection of caste, where all sit together on the floor and share one meal.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the elephant that would not charge, and your line, the elephant bowed. Did you stand still for one breath before something big? Today Kabir stands his ground with words. Day seven hundred fifty-two.

A question can do what an argument can't. Ask someone, where were you born, and you learn a city. Ask, how were you born, and everyone in the room gives the same answer. Same way in. Same cry. Same small, wet, helpless start. A weaver in Kashi once took that plain fact and turned it into a question for a learned man who thought his birth made him higher. The question is still sitting in the Guru Granth Sahib, in Raag Gauri, waiting for whoever reads it. Today: if you're a Brahmin.
screen: `WHERE WERE YOU BORN?` → `HOW WERE YOU BORN?` → `THE SAME WAY IN.`

segments.voice: Kabir starts in the womb. In the womb, he says, there's no family line and no caste. Everyone comes from the same seed of the Divine. Then he turns to the pandit, the learned man, and asks: tell me, since when have you been a Brahmin? Don't waste your life just saying the word. And then the question from today's title. If you're a Brahmin, born of a Brahmin mother, why didn't you come into the world by some other road? He presses it with a picture. How are you a Brahmin and I a Shudra? Is it blood in my veins and milk in yours? You can hear the weaver's humor in it. He isn't shouting. He's asking a question so plain that pride has nowhere to stand. Now the part that keeps this from being an attack on anyone. Kabir doesn't throw away the word Brahmin. He gives it a new meaning. The hymn ends: Kabir says, whoever reflects on God, that one we call a Brahmin. So the line isn't against a people or a faith. It's against the idea that birth decides worth. Sikhs hear this hymn beside the Gurus' own teaching, which also refused to rank people by caste, and beside the langar, where everyone sits on the same floor and eats the same food. Today's line is the fact Kabir starts from. Whatever titles come later, every one of us was born the same way.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: meet someone as an equal. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person you tend to look up to too much, or down on without noticing. A boss, a cleaner, a celebrity, a cousin. Picture them as Kabir does: arriving in the world the same way you did, small and crying. Hold that picture for a few breaths. Then picture them now, and see if anything has leveled out. If you pray, you can say Waheguru once for them and once for you. The bell holds the time.
If you're a Brahmin. Kabir's question in Raag Gauri: if birth made you high, why weren't you born by some other road?

753.title: Don't call the scriptures false
753.hook: don't call the Vedas and the Semitic books false; false is the one who doesn't reflect (Prabhati, Kabir, ang 1350)
753.tomorrow: I am the worst of all
753.howItsDone: Sikhs sing this Prabhati hymn of Kabir in kirtan, and Sikh teachers use its line on the Vedas and the Kateb to call listeners to reflect on scripture rather than dismiss anyone's.

segments.voice: Yesterday, if you're a Brahmin, and your line, born the same way. Did you greet someone you'd usually pass by? Today Kabir turns from birth to books. Day seven hundred fifty-three.

Two shelves. On one, the Vedas, the old hymns of the Hindu tradition. On the other, the Kateb, Kabir's word for the books of the Muslim neighbors, the Qur'an among them. A weaver who has just told a proud man that birth makes no one higher might be expected to sweep both shelves onto the floor. If caste doesn't count, maybe the books don't either. That's not what he does. In a hymn in Raag Prabhati, Kabir draws a line in a very different place. Today: don't call the scriptures false.
screen: `TWO SHELVES.` → `THE VEDAS AND THE KATEB.` → `A LINE IN A DIFFERENT PLACE.`

segments.voice: Kabir's hymns in Raag Prabhati sit close together on the page. One opens wide. First, Kabir sings, God made the light, and from that one light the whole creation came. So who is good and who is bad? Then, in a neighboring hymn, comes the line in today's title. Don't say the Vedas and the Kateb are false, he says. False is the one who doesn't reflect. Read that twice, because it moves the problem. The danger isn't sitting on the shelf. It's sitting in the reader. A book can be read with care or with no thought at all. Someone can carry a holy text everywhere and never once stop to think about what it asks. Kabir points his finger there, not at the pages. And notice what he isn't saying. He isn't saying all books say the same thing. He isn't asking anyone to give up their own. He's naming a habit: dismissing a scripture you haven't sat with, or reciting your own without letting it reach you. Both skip the same step. The word in the line is bichar, to reflect, to think something through. Sikh teachers say the Guru's word asks to be understood, not only recited. Read that way, Kabir's line asks the same of every reader, whatever shelf they read from: sit with a line before calling a book empty, and let your own book reach you before calling it full. That's today's carry: reflect, don't dismiss.
screen: `FROM ONE LIGHT, THE WHOLE CREATION.` · `FALSE IS THE ONE WHO DOESN'T REFLECT.` · `THE DANGER SITS IN THE READER.` · `BICHAR: THINK IT THROUGH.` · then, large: `REFLECT, DON'T DISMISS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: reflect on one line of any scripture. Your own, a neighbor's, one you've only heard quoted. Settle, and breathe. Bring one line to mind. If none comes, use today's: false is the one who doesn't reflect. Say it slowly, inside. Then ask it one question: what is this asking of me today? Don't argue with it, and don't rush to agree. Just turn it over, the way you'd turn a stone in your hand. If you pray, you can say Waheguru before and after. The bell holds the time.
Don't call the scriptures false. Kabir's line in Raag Prabhati: don't call the Vedas and the Kateb false; false is the one who doesn't reflect.

segments.voice: Your line: reflect, don't dismiss. Today, when you're about to wave off an idea or a book, give it one honest minute of thought first. Day seven hundred fifty-three.

754.title: I am the worst of all
754.word: I am the worst of all
754.hook: Kabir says he is the worst, and everyone else is good (Kabir salok, ang 1364)
754.howItsDone: Sikhs read and sing Kabir's saloks, gathered near the end of the Guru Granth Sahib, and teachers use this one to teach nimrata, humility, alongside the Gurus' own hymns.

segments.voice: Yesterday, don't call the scriptures false, and your line, reflect, don't dismiss. Which idea did you give one honest minute? Today Kabir turns that same reflection on himself. Day seven hundred fifty-four.

A group chat goes sour. Someone said something careless, someone else snapped, and now everyone is typing out exactly who did what wrong. Screenshots. Receipts. Every message pointing outward. Now set beside that scene a couplet, two short lines, from the back of the Guru Granth Sahib, where Kabir's saloks are gathered. It points the other way entirely. It's so blunt it can sound almost wrong on first hearing. Today: I am the worst of all.
screen: `A GROUP CHAT GOES SOUR.` → `EVERY FINGER POINTS OUT.` → `A COUPLET POINTS IN.`

segments.voice: Here's the salok. Kabir, it begins, I am the worst of all; apart from me, everyone is good. And the second line: whoever comes to see it this way is my friend. That's the whole of it. Two lines. Now, it would be easy to hear this as someone who hates himself. Sikh teachers read it differently. They hear humility, the low, open place where water gathers. Kabir isn't keeping a score where he loses. He's refusing to keep the score at all. Think about where the eye goes in that group chat. Outward, to everyone else's faults, because that's where the eye naturally points. Farid's couplet, a little over two weeks back on this path, said look inside your own collar. Kabir's salok turns the same way and follows it all the way down. Look at your own part first, so carefully that by the time you're done, you've run out of energy for judging anyone else. And the second line matters as much as the first. Whoever sees it this way is my friend. So it's not a lonely practice. It's the ground of a friendship: two people who've both stopped pointing. Guru Nanak, in Raag Suhi, says we are not good, and no one is bad. That's the shape of it. Not crushing yourself. Just taking yourself off the judge's bench. Here's the surprise in it. The salok says I am the worst, but the line it hands us to carry is the other half: everyone else is good. The point isn't the low opinion of yourself. It's the generous eye it frees up for everyone else.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look for your own fault first. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one recent friction: an argument, a cold silence, a sharp text. Before you think about what they did, find your part. Even a small one. A tone, a delay, an assumption. Name it to yourself, plainly, without punishing yourself for it. Then notice how the other person looks once your part is on the table. If you pray, you can say Waheguru, and let it be gentle. The bell holds the time.

755.title: The Lord's dog
755.hook: Kabir calls himself the Lord's dog, with a chain round his neck, going where He leads (Kabir salok, ang 1368)
755.howItsDone: Sikhs read Kabir's saloks near the end of the Guru Granth Sahib, and teachers use this one to speak of hukam, walking in the Divine will with trust rather than resistance.

segments.voice: Yesterday, I am the worst of all, and your line, everyone else is good. Did you find your own part before you named someone else's? Today Kabir lowers himself again, this time with a smile. Day seven hundred fifty-five.

Early morning, any street. A dog trots ahead of its person, nose down, tail up, stopping at every post. Then a gentle tug on the leash, and the dog turns, without fuss, and goes the other way. It doesn't sulk. It doesn't argue. It knows whose hand is on the other end. Kabir saw that too, and he put himself in the picture. In one of his saloks he doesn't call himself a saint, or a seeker, or even a weaver. He gives himself a name, and a collar. Today: the Lord's dog.
screen: `A DOG TROTS AHEAD.` → `A GENTLE TUG.` → `IT KNOWS WHOSE HAND IT IS.`

segments.voice: Here's the salok. Kabir, I am the Lord's dog, and Moti is my name. There's a cord around my neck; wherever He pulls me, I go. Moti means pearl. It's a pet's name, the kind you'd call across a yard. So Kabir isn't only lowering himself here. He's also saying he's loved. A dog with a name belongs to someone. Calling yourself a dog was no flattering thing. And Kabir chose it anyway, with a little warmth and maybe a little humor. Yesterday he said, I am the worst of all. Today he says something close, but the feeling has shifted. It's less about faults and more about trust. A dog on a leash isn't ashamed. It's attached. Now the chain. It could sound like a prison. But listen to who's holding it, and how Kabir answers: wherever He pulls me, I go. No complaint in it. The chain is what keeps him near. Sikh teachers connect this with hukam, the Divine will, and the Gurus' call to walk in it. Not dragged, but led. There's even relief in it. A dog doesn't have to plan the whole walk. It only has to feel the next tug and follow. Kabir doesn't pretend the leash isn't there. He just knows whose hand it's in. So today's carry isn't about being bound. It's about being close enough to feel where you're being taken. Led by the chain.
screen: `I AM THE LORD'S DOG.` · `MOTI: A PEARL, A PET'S NAME.` · `WHEREVER HE PULLS ME, I GO.` · `HUKAM: NOT DRAGGED, BUT LED.` · then, large: `LED BY THE CHAIN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: follow one good lead. Settle, and breathe. Think of a small nudge you've been feeling and ignoring. Call your grandmother. Drink some water. Apologize. Go to bed earlier. Don't plan the whole walk. Just feel the tug, the next small step, and agree to it. Let your breath be easy, like a dog trotting beside someone it trusts. If you pray, you can say Waheguru, and let it be your yes. The bell holds the time.
The Lord's dog. Kabir's salok: Moti is my name, there's a cord around my neck, and wherever He pulls me, I go.
Your line: led by the chain. Today, when you feel a small good tug, a kind thing to do or a word to say, follow it before you talk yourself out of it. Day seven hundred fifty-five.

756.title: Dead while alive
756.hook: Kabir speaks of dying to ego while still living, and so being free
756.howItsDone: Sikhs speak of jeevan mukat as freedom from ego while living an ordinary householder's life, and Kabir's saloks on dying to the self are sung and explained in kirtan and katha.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Lord's dog, and your line, led by the chain. Did you follow one small good tug? It's the end of a week with Kabir: a mother's tears, an elephant, a proud man, two shelves of books, a dog named Moti. Day seven hundred fifty-six.

Some people go quiet when the subject of dying comes up. Change the topic. Knock on wood. Kabir does something stranger. He talks about death as if it were good news. Not someday, at the end, but now, today, while the heart is still beating. For two days he's been lowering himself: the worst of all, the Lord's dog. Today we find out where that road goes. It goes somewhere that sounds, at first, like a contradiction. Today: dead while alive.
screen: `SOME PEOPLE CHANGE THE TOPIC.` → `KABIR CALLS IT GOOD NEWS.` → `WHERE THE LOW ROAD GOES.`

segments.voice: Here's one of Kabir's saloks. The dying that the world fears, he says, brings joy to my mind. Because it's through dying that perfect bliss is found. Now, Kabir isn't longing for a funeral. Sikh readers hear in this a different death: the death of the ego, the I that grabs and compares and insists on its own way. Haumai, Sikhs call it, the sense of I, me, mine. It's the thing that kept a proud man sure his birth made him higher. It's the thing that points at everyone else's faults. This week's hymns have been slowly loosening it. When it finally lets go, something is left that's lighter and freer, and still breathing. That's today's word. Jeevan mukat. Jeevan is life. Mukat is freedom, release. Free while living. Sikh teaching doesn't place freedom only after death, in some far-off place. It can be tasted here, at the kitchen sink, at the loom, in traffic. The person who's free while living still works, still eats, still loves their family. Kabir kept singing. What has died is the grip. Try it with your hands. You're holding a hot pan by the handle, knuckles white, scared to drop it. Now set it down. Your hand is still your hand. It's just not clenched anymore. That's the kind of dying Kabir is talking about: the clench goes, the hand stays. So the line we carry out of this week is not about the end of life. It's about the middle of it. Free while living.
screen: `THE DYING THE WORLD FEARS.` · `HAUMAI: I, ME, MINE.` · `JEEVAN MUKAT: FREE WHILE LIVING.` · `THE CLENCH GOES, THE HAND STAYS.` · then, large: `FREE WHILE LIVING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let one ego-want go. Settle, and breathe. Find one small thing your I is gripping right now. Wanting the last word. Wanting credit. Wanting someone to notice you were right. Don't fight it. Just name it, and on each out-breath, loosen your hold by a little, like setting down a hot pan. See what's left when the clench goes. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each out-breath. The bell holds the time.
Jeevan mukat. Free while living: released from the grip of ego here and now, not only after death.
Your line: free while living. Look back over this week with Kabir, and let one grip from it go today, a grudge, a need to win, a fear of what people think. Day seven hundred fifty-six.
